scenes.heading: Two ways atoms bond together
scenes.narration: Atoms connect by either ionic bonding or covalent bonding. While ionic bonds involve a complete electron transfer from one atom to another, covalent bonds involve atoms that simply share electrons to gain stability.

scenes.heading: Which atoms join which way
scenes.narration: Ionic links usually form between a metal and a non-metal because their pull on electrons is very different. Meanwhile, covalent links typically happen when two non-metals meet, as neither can pull hard enough to steal.

scenes.heading: Lattices versus separate molecules
scenes.narration: The transfer creates charged ions that lock into a massive alternating lattice. On the other hand, sharing forms discrete, independent molecules held together as small, separate units rather than a giant crystal structure.

scenes.heading: Melting points and electricity
scenes.narration: Because those lattice bonds are so strong, ionic substances have a high melting point and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved. Covalent substances have low melting points and typically do not conduct electricity well.

scenes.heading: Sodium chloride and water
scenes.narration: As a worked example, sodium chloride forms an ionic lattice of charged particles. Water forms covalent molecules where hydrogen and oxygen atoms share electrons to create stable, independent units.
